meta.title: Mental Imagery in Depression: Phenomenology, Potential Mechanisms, and Treatment Implications
meta.domain: Clinical psychology — mental imagery in depression (review)
meta.overview: Annual Review synthesizing the role of mental imagery in depression: an excess of intrusive negative imagery and a deficit of vivid positive/prospective imagery, links to observer-perspective bias and overgeneral autobiographical memory, imagery's amplified emotional impact relative to verbal thought, and imagery-based treatments (rescripting, positive-imagery cognitive bias modification, memory specificity training).
meta.abstract: Depression is characterized by an excess of intrusive negative mental imagery and a deficit in vivid positive/prospective imagery. This review covers the phenomenology of imagery in depression (including observer-perspective bias and overgeneral memory), evidence that imagery has a stronger impact on emotion than verbal processing, candidate mechanisms, and imagery-focused treatment implications including imagery rescripting and positive-imagery cognitive bias modification.

claims.statement: Depression is characterized by an excess of intrusive negative mental imagery and impoverished positive/prospective imagery.
Imagery abnormalities in depression include an observer-perspective bias and overgeneral autobiographical memory.
Mental imagery has a more powerful impact on emotion than verbal (word-based) processing.
Imagery-based interventions (imagery rescripting, positive-imagery cognitive bias modification, memory specificity training) are candidate treatments for depression.
Overgeneral autobiographical memory is a vulnerability marker predicting the course of depressive symptoms.

quantities.quote: after three episodes, the risk of further episodes is 90% (see, e.g., Bockting et al. 2015)
approximately 50% of patients with depression do not respond to treatment
Patel and colleagues (2007) found that almost half of a depressed sample reported frequent distressing intrusive images of memories or imagined events.
lifetime prevalence estimates ranging from 16.6% (Kessler et al. 2005)

contributions.typing_rationale: Annual Review integrating phenomenology, mechanisms, and treatment of mental imagery in depression, shifting the field from verbal-descriptive to depictive (imagery) formats and linking overgeneral memory to imagery deficits.

sota.resolver_notes: Undermind semantic search (year_max=2016) surfaced the immediate neighborhood as the emerging imagery-in-depression line: Wheatley 2007 (imagery rescripting of intrusive memories in depression), a 2013 CBM+imagery treatment strand, and Wells-style 2014 (visual imagery in psychopathology), with Holmes 2008 (imagery as emotional amplifier) as the mechanistic parent. As an Annual Review it has high overlap with — and synthesizes — this prior work.
